newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia needs to import wheat - commerce chamber.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia needs to import wheat - commerce chamber.

text.p: Yugoslavia will have to import an unspecified amount of wheat this year, an official at the Serbian Chamber of Commerce said on Thursday.
"There is not enough wheat in the country's reserves," Rada Vujanov of the chamber's board for agriculture told Reuters. "There is not enough wheat to feed the people."
Parliament was to discuss the import quota for wheat at its regular Thursday session. A source close to the government said it could be as much as 300,000 tonnes.
Analysts and officials privately conceded the government's stockpiles of wheat were lower than it had admitted and insufficient to feed the country's population of 10 million.
According to official estimates, Yugoslavia needs at least two million tonnes of wheat for its consumption each year.
For the first time this year, the state agency for commodity reserves declined to disclose how much wheat it had bought from farmers.
Officials have accused the federal government of wasting available wheat stocks and artificially depressing supply by not offering farmers enough money for their crops.
"Where will the government find money for imports when they cannot pay farmers for their sugar beet or sunflower?" said Zlatica Markovic of the Yugoslav association of mills and bakeries.

"We are paying the bill for low investments in agricultural production and the government's poor record of payments to farmers for the 1995 wheat harvest," said the head of the Yugoslav grains fund, Vukosav Sakovic.

He added the first import deal had already been concluded and was being directed to Novi Sad port, but declined to give According to figures supplied by the chamber's board for agricuture, this year's wheat harvest plunged to a 40-year low of just 1.51 million tonnes, almost half the 2.97 million recorded in 1995.

Yields dropped to 2.6 tonnes per hectare from an average of 4.22 in 1989 to 1991. This, coupled with a 30 percent drop in wheat area to 583,000 hectares and extremely unfavourable weather, accounted for the meagre harvest.
But an official at the Serbian agriculture ministry said the government should be careful not to set too high an import quota.
"We expect at least 3.5 million tonnes of wheat from the 1997 harvest," he said. "That's 1.5 million tonnes of surplus."
